LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Thymus:
Overview — The T-Cell School

The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ — the site where T cells mature and are “educated”. It is a bilobed organ in the anterior mediastinum, largest at puberty, after which it involutes and is replaced by fat.

🔬 Image slot — thymus at low power — lobules with a dark T-cell-rich cortex, a pale medulla, and Hassall's corpuscles

It develops from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch: an epithelial framework (from endoderm) colonised by lymphoid cells (from bone marrow).

Unlike a lymph node, the thymus has no B-cell follicles, no germinal centres and no afferent lymphatics — it is a T-cell factory, not a filter.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — thymic lobule — densely packed cortical thymocytes, a paler medulla, and a concentric keratinised Hassall's corpuscle
  • Lobules with an outer dark cortex (densely packed thymocytes) and an inner pale medulla.
  • Hassall’s (thymic) corpuscles in the medulla — concentric whorls of keratinised epithelial cells — the diagnostic feature.
  • No lymphoid follicles or germinal centres (contrast with lymph node/spleen).
Dark cortex + pale medulla + Hassall’s corpuscles → thymus. Hassall’s corpuscles alone clinch it — nothing else in the body looks like them.
Cortex, Medulla & Hassall’s Corpuscles
Cortex (dark)
  • Densely packed immature thymocytes (T cells)
  • Contains the blood–thymus barrier
  • Site of positive selection
Medulla (pale)
  • Fewer, more mature T cells
  • Contains Hassall’s corpuscles
  • Site of negative selection
  • Hassall’s corpuscles are concentric, keratinised aggregates of epithelial reticular cells; they increase with age and help regulate T-cell development.
The cortex is dark because it is crammed with maturing thymocytes; the medulla is pale. Hassall’s corpuscles mark the medulla.
Epithelial Reticular Cells & T-Cell Selection
🔬 Image slot — T-cell selection — positive selection in the cortex (recognise self-MHC) and negative selection in the medulla (delete self-reactive cells)
  • Epithelial reticular cells form the supporting framework (not reticular fibres), make thymic hormones (thymosin, thymopoietin), build the blood–thymus barrier, and present MHC for T-cell selection.
1
Positive selection (cortex)keep T cells that recognise self-MHC
2
Negative selection (medulla)delete T cells strongly reactive to self-antigen
3
Central toleranceonly self-tolerant, MHC-restricted T cells leave
Medullary cells use the AIRE gene to display peripheral self-antigens for negative selection. AIRE mutation → multi-organ autoimmunity (APECED).
Age Involution
  • The thymus is largest at puberty, then progressively involutes: thymic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue and thymocyte numbers fall.
  • T-cell output declines with age, but the peripheral T-cell pool is already established.
Age involution (fatty replacement) is normal; do not mistake a fatty adult thymus for pathology.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
DiGeorge syndrome
22q11 deletion → thymic aplasia/hypoplasia → T-cell immunodeficiency (+ hypocalcaemia, cardiac defects)
Thymoma
Epithelial tumour; associated with myasthenia gravis, pure red-cell aplasia & hypogammaglobulinaemia
Myasthenia gravis
Thymic hyperplasia or thymoma; anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies; may improve after thymectomy
SCID
Severe combined immunodeficiency — failure of T-cell (± B-cell) development
APECED (AIRE mutation)
Failed negative selection → autoimmune polyendocrinopathy
Thymic (follicular) hyperplasia
Germinal centres appear in the medulla — associated with autoimmune disease
⭐ Exam Pearls
Dark cortex + pale medulla + Hassall’s corpuscles = thymus.
Hassall’s corpuscles (medulla) = diagnostic: concentric keratinised epithelial cells.
Primary lymphoid organ for T-cell maturation — no B follicles, germinal centres or afferent lymphatics.
Positive selection = cortex (recognise self-MHC); negative selection = medulla (delete self-reactive; AIRE).
Epithelial reticular cells form the framework + blood–thymus barrier + thymic hormones (thymosin).
Largest at puberty, then involutes (replaced by fat) — a normal change.
DiGeorge (22q11) = thymic aplasia → T-cell deficiency; thymoma → myasthenia gravis.
AIRE mutation → failed negative selection → APECED autoimmunity.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Lymph Node:
Overview — The Lymph Filter & Immune Hub

The lymph node is a secondary lymphoid organ: it filters lymph and is where adaptive immune responses are generated (antigen presentation, B- and T-cell activation). It is a bean-shaped, encapsulated organ arranged in three zones.

🔬 Image slot — lymph node at low power — capsule, subcapsular sinus, cortex with follicles, deep paracortex, and central medulla with a hilum
1
CortexB-cell follicles
2
ParacortexT cells + high endothelial venules
3
Medullamedullary cords (plasma cells) + sinuses
Learn it as a map: B cells in the cortical follicles, T cells in the paracortex, plasma cells in the medulla — and lymph flowing through sinuses from surface to hilum.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — lymph node cortex — capsule, subcapsular sinus, and a secondary follicle with a pale germinal centre and dark mantle zone
  • A dense connective-tissue capsule with a subcapsular sinus beneath it.
  • Cortical follicles — rounded B-cell aggregates, often with pale germinal centres.
  • A diffuse paracortex (T cells) and a central medulla of cords and sinuses.
Capsule + subcapsular sinus + cortical follicles + paracortex + medulla → lymph node. A germinal centre with a “starry-sky” look confirms an active B-cell response.
Cortex, Paracortex & Medulla
Cortex (follicles)
B cells; primary follicles (no germinal centre) vs secondary follicles (active germinal centre + mantle zone)
Paracortex (deep cortex)
T cells + high endothelial venules (HEVs) where lymphocytes enter from blood; interdigitating dendritic cells
Medulla
Medullary cords (plasma cells, B cells, macrophages) between medullary sinuses
B-cortex, T-paracortex, plasma-cell medulla. The paracortex expands in viral infection (T-cell response); the follicles expand in B-cell responses.
Lymph Flow & the Sinus System
🔬 Image slot — lymph flow — multiple afferent lymphatics on the convex surface, through subcapsular and medullary sinuses, to a single efferent vessel at the hilum
1
Afferent lymphaticsmany, on the convex surface
2
Subcapsular → trabecular → medullary sinusesmacrophages filter antigen/debris
3
Efferent lymphaticsingle, leaves at the hilum
  • Many afferents in, one efferent out — and valves keep flow one-way; the artery and vein enter/leave at the hilum.
  • HEVs in the paracortex are the entry point for blood-borne lymphocytes recirculating into the node.
Because lymph enters through the subcapsular sinus, metastatic tumour cells seed the subcapsular sinus first — a key staging fact.
The Germinal Centre & Reactive Patterns
  • A germinal centre (secondary follicle) is a site of B-cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation, supported by follicular dendritic cells.
  • Tingible-body macrophages clearing apoptotic B cells give the “starry-sky” appearance.
  • Output: high-affinity plasma cells (to the medulla) and memory B cells.
Follicular hyperplasia
  • B-cell response (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, early HIV)
Paracortical hyperplasia
  • T-cell response (viral infections, drug reactions)
Reactive follicular hyperplasia keeps a preserved architecture & polarised germinal centres with tingible-body macrophages — features that help distinguish it from follicular lymphoma.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Reactive lymphadenopathy
Follicular (B), paracortical (viral/drug) or sinus histiocytosis patterns; architecture preserved
Hodgkin lymphoma
Reed–Sternberg cells (“owl-eye”, CD15/CD30+); orderly contiguous spread
Follicular lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin B-cell; t(14;18) overexpressing BCL2; back-to-back follicles
Burkitt lymphoma
t(8;14) MYC; very high turnover with a “starry-sky” pattern
Metastatic carcinoma
Seeds the subcapsular sinus first; basis of sentinel-node biopsy
Granulomatous lymphadenitis
Caseating (TB) vs non-caseating (sarcoidosis) granulomas
Loss of the normal nodal architecture (effacement) by a monotonous cell population points to lymphoma rather than reactive change.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Capsule + subcapsular sinus + cortical follicles + paracortex + medulla = lymph node.
B-cortex (follicles), T-paracortex (+ HEVs), plasma-cell medulla.
Germinal centre = active B-cell response; tingible-body macrophages give the starry sky.
HEVs in the paracortex are where blood lymphocytes enter the node.
Lymph flow: many afferents (convex) → sinuses → one efferent (hilum); valves keep it one-way.
Metastases seed the subcapsular sinus first (sentinel node principle).
Follicular hyperplasia = B (RA, HIV); paracortical hyperplasia = T (viral/drug).
Reed–Sternberg = Hodgkin; follicular lymphoma t(14;18)/BCL2; Burkitt t(8;14)/MYC starry sky.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Spleen:
Overview — The Blood Filter

The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ and the only one that filters blood rather than lymph. It does two jobs, held in two “pulps”:

🔬 Image slot — spleen at low power — scattered white pulp nodules (each around a central arteriole) within a sea of red pulp, under a capsule with trabeculae
White pulp
  • Immune function — lymphocytes around arterioles
  • Responds to blood-borne antigen
Red pulp
  • Filtration — removes old/damaged red cells
  • Recycles iron; stores platelets
Unlike a lymph node, the spleen has no cortex/medulla and no afferent lymphatics — its white pulp is organised around central arterioles.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — splenic tissue — a white pulp nodule with its eccentric central arteriole and germinal centre, surrounded by red pulp cords and sinusoids
  • Red pulp everywhere (the majority) — red-cell-filled cords and sinusoids.
  • White pulp nodules scattered within it, each built around a central arteriole.
  • A capsule (dense connective tissue with some smooth muscle) sending in trabeculae.
White pulp around a central arteriole + red pulp of cords & sinusoids → spleen. The eccentric central arteriole in a lymphoid nodule is the giveaway.
White Pulp — The Immune Compartment
PALS
Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of T cells wrapped around the central arteriole
Lymphoid follicles
B cells (with germinal centres) attached to the PALS
Marginal zone
Interface with the red pulp; macrophages, dendritic & marginal-zone B cells sample blood antigen and admit lymphocytes
PALS = T cells; follicles = B cells; marginal zone = the antigen-sampling border where blood-borne antigen first meets the immune system.
Red Pulp & Red-Cell Filtering
🔬 Image slot — red pulp — splenic cords of Billroth with macrophages between sinusoids lined by elongated stave cells and a discontinuous basement membrane
Splenic cords (of Billroth)
  • Loose reticular meshwork packed with macrophages
Splenic sinusoids
  • Lined by elongated stave cells with gaps + discontinuous basement membrane
  • Force red cells to squeeze through
  • Red cells must deform to pass from the cords into the sinusoids; old/damaged cells that can’t deform are phagocytosed (culling).
  • Pitting removes intracellular inclusions (Howell–Jolly bodies, Heinz bodies) without destroying the cell; iron is recycled.
This slow, tortuous passage through the cords is the “open” splenic circulation — the mechanical test that culls aged and abnormal red cells.
Circulation & Functions
1
Central arterioleruns through the white pulp (PALS)
2
Penicillar arterioles → cordsopen circulation into the red pulp
3
Sinusoids → splenic veinfiltered blood returns
  • Immune: mounts responses to blood-borne antigens (marginal zone & white pulp).
  • Haematological: culls/pits red cells, recycles iron, stores ~1/3 of platelets and monocytes, and can resume extramedullary haematopoiesis.
The spleen is a reservoir: it holds about a third of the body’s platelets and a large monocyte pool it can release on demand.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Hyposplenism / splenectomy
Blood film shows Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells & thrombocytosis; risk of overwhelming infection
OPSI
Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection by encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) → vaccinate + prophylaxis
Splenomegaly
Portal hypertension, infections (malaria, EBV), haematological disease, storage disorders
Hypersplenism
Overactive sequestration → cytopenias (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia)
Sickle cell / autosplenectomy
Repeated infarction destroys the spleen → functional asplenia
Traumatic rupture / ITP
Rupture → haemorrhage; in ITP the spleen removes antibody-coated platelets
Howell–Jolly bodies on a blood film = the spleen is not working (absent or hypofunctional) — because pitting normally removes them.
⭐ Exam Pearls
White pulp around a central arteriole + red pulp of cords & sinusoids = spleen.
The spleen filters blood, not lymph — no cortex/medulla, no afferent lymphatics.
White pulp: PALS = T cells; follicles = B cells; marginal zone = antigen sampling.
Red pulp: cords of Billroth (macrophages) + sinusoids (stave cells, discontinuous BM) filter red cells.
Culling removes old red cells; pitting removes inclusions (Howell–Jolly, Heinz bodies).
Reservoir of ~1/3 of platelets & monocytes; can resume extramedullary haematopoiesis.
Hyposplenism → Howell–Jolly bodies + risk from encapsulated organisms (OPSI) → vaccinate.
Hypersplenism → cytopenias; sickle cell → autosplenectomy.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Tonsils:
Overview — Gatekeepers of Waldeyer’s Ring

The tonsils are aggregates of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) forming a defensive ring (Waldeyer’s ring) at the entrance to the pharynx. They sample ingested and inhaled antigen and mount local (IgA) immune responses.

🔬 Image slot — tonsil at low power — surface epithelium dipping into deep crypts, with subepithelial lymphoid follicles bearing germinal centres
  • Waldeyer’s ring = palatine + pharyngeal (adenoid) + lingual + tubal tonsils.
  • They are partially encapsulated and, like all MALT, have no afferent lymphatics — antigen is sampled directly through the epithelium.
The signature is epithelium that dips into crypts over a bed of lymphoid follicles with germinal centres.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — tonsillar tissue — stratified squamous epithelium lining branching crypts, dense subepithelial follicles with germinal centres, and a partial capsule
  • Surface epithelium invaginating into crypts — the defining architecture.
  • Subepithelial lymphoid follicles with germinal centres packed beneath the epithelium.
  • A partial (incomplete) capsule on the deep surface; crypts may contain debris/detritus.
Crypt-bearing epithelium over follicles with germinal centres → tonsil. Identify the epithelial type to name which tonsil (squamous vs respiratory).
The Tonsils of Waldeyer’s Ring
🔬 Image slot — comparison — palatine (squamous, deep branching crypts), pharyngeal/adenoid (respiratory ciliated epithelium, folds), and lingual tonsils
Palatine tonsils
Paired, between the tonsillar arches; stratified squamous epithelium; 10–20 deep branching crypts; partial capsule — the “tonsillitis” tonsils
Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid)
Single, roof of the nasopharynx; respiratory pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; folds rather than deep crypts
Lingual tonsils
Base of the tongue; stratified squamous epithelium; a single crypt each
Palatine & lingual = stratified squamous; pharyngeal (adenoid) = respiratory ciliated epithelium. Deep, branching crypts point to the palatine tonsil.
Crypts, Antigen Sampling & MALT Function
  • Crypts hugely increase the surface area over which antigen contacts the lymphoid tissue — they trap food/microbial antigen (and debris).
  • The epithelium is infiltrated by lymphocytes and specialised antigen-transporting (M-like) cells that ferry antigen to the underlying follicles.
  • Germinal centres generate a B-cell response producing secretory IgA for mucosal defence.
  • There are no afferent lymphatics; lymphocytes/antibody drain via efferent vessels to the cervical lymph nodes.
Tonsils are MALT: they sample antigen directly through their epithelium (no afferent lymph), unlike a lymph node that filters incoming lymph.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Tonsillitis
Viral or bacterial (Group A Streptococcus); exudate in the crypts; Centor criteria guide antibiotics
Quinsy
Peritonsillar abscess → trismus, “hot-potato” voice, uvular deviation — needs drainage
Adenoidal hypertrophy
Enlarged pharyngeal tonsil in children → nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, OSA & glue ear
Infectious mononucleosis
EBV; enlarged exudative tonsils, cervical lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes
Tonsillar carcinoma
HPV-related (p16+) oropharyngeal SCC arising in the crypt epithelium; better prognosis than HPV-negative
Tonsilloliths
Calcified debris in the crypts (“tonsil stones”) causing halitosis
A persistently unilateral enlarged tonsil in an adult is a red flag for malignancy (lymphoma or HPV-related SCC) and warrants investigation.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Crypt-bearing epithelium over follicles with germinal centres = tonsil (MALT).
Waldeyer’s ring = palatine + pharyngeal (adenoid) + lingual + tubal tonsils.
Palatine & lingual = stratified squamous; pharyngeal (adenoid) = respiratory ciliated columnar.
Deep branching crypts = palatine tonsil (the “tonsillitis” tonsils).
Partially encapsulated; no afferent lymphatics — antigen sampled directly through the epithelium.
Germinal centres produce secretory IgA; drainage is to the cervical nodes.
Adenoidal hypertrophy → nasal obstruction / OSA / glue ear; quinsy = peritonsillar abscess.
HPV/p16 oropharyngeal SCC arises in tonsillar crypts; unilateral tonsil enlargement is a red flag.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Mucosa-Associated Lym:
Overview — Frontline Mucosal Immunity

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is unencapsulated lymphoid tissue in the mucosae of the gut, airways and urogenital tract. It is the immune system’s frontline where the outside world meets the body, and its main product is secretory IgA.

🔬 Image slot — MALT — unencapsulated lymphoid follicles with germinal centres in the mucosa, beneath a follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells
  • Regional names: GALT (gut — Peyer’s patches, appendix, tonsils), BALT (bronchial), NALT (nasal).
  • It exists as organised follicles and as diffuse scattered lymphocytes/plasma cells.
The defining traits: no capsule, no afferent lymphatics, and a specialised M-cell epithelium that samples luminal antigen directly.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — gut MALT — a lymphoid follicle with a germinal centre in the lamina propria/submucosa, a dome region, and follicle-associated epithelium lacking villi
  • Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres sitting in the lamina propria/submucosa — with no capsule around them.
  • An overlying follicle-associated epithelium (FAE) forming a dome, lacking villi and goblet cells.
  • Diffuse lymphocytes and plasma cells scattered through the lamina propria.
Unencapsulated germinal-centre follicles in a mucosa, under a specialised dome epithelium → MALT. In the ileum this is a Peyer’s patch.
Organised vs Diffuse MALT
Organised MALT
  • Peyer’s patches (ileum), appendix, tonsils, isolated lymphoid follicles
  • Discrete follicles with germinal centres + interfollicular T zones
Diffuse MALT
  • Scattered lymphocytes & plasma cells in the lamina propria
  • The “effector” arm secreting antibody locally
  • Peyer’s patches are the classic example: submucosal follicles in the ileum that bulge into the mucosa, with a dome epithelium and no villi over the dome.
Organised MALT (Peyer’s patches, tonsils, appendix) inducts the response; diffuse lamina-propria plasma cells deliver the antibody.
M Cells, the Dome Epithelium & Secretory IgA
🔬 Image slot — M cell — sampling luminal antigen and transcytosing it to dendritic cells and lymphocytes in the subepithelial pocket
1
M cell samples antigentranscytosis across the follicle-associated epithelium
2
Presented to lymphocytesdendritic cells & B/T cells in the dome
3
Plasma cells make dimeric IgAtransported into the lumen as secretory IgA
  • M (microfold) cells are the antigen gateway — they lack a brush border and transcytose luminal antigen to the immune cells beneath.
  • Plasma cells secrete dimeric IgA, which is carried across the epithelium by the poly-Ig receptor and released with its secretory component as secretory IgA.
M cells sample; plasma cells respond with secretory IgA. The secretory component protects IgA from digestion in the harsh luminal environment.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Gastric MALT lymphoma
Extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma driven by H. pylori; often regresses with eradication
MALT lymphoma (other sites)
Salivary gland (Sjögren’s), thyroid (Hashimoto’s), lung — from chronic antigen stimulation
Peyer’s patch as a portal
Entry route for Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia and prions (vCJD) via M cells
Selective IgA deficiency
Commonest primary immunodeficiency → mucosal/respiratory/GI infections; risk of anaphylaxis to blood products
Coeliac disease
Increased intra-epithelial lymphocytes reflect mucosal immune activation
Appendicitis
Lymphoid (GALT) hyperplasia can obstruct the appendiceal lumen, precipitating inflammation
The stomach normally has little MALT — it is acquired in response to H. pylori, which is why eradication can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Unencapsulated germinal-centre follicles in a mucosa + M-cell dome epithelium = MALT.
Regional MALT: GALT (Peyer’s patches, appendix, tonsils), BALT, NALT.
Peyer’s patches = ileum; submucosal follicles under a dome epithelium with no villi.
M (microfold) cells sample luminal antigen — no afferent lymphatics needed.
Main product = secretory IgA (dimeric IgA + secretory component via the poly-Ig receptor).
MALT lymphoma arises from chronic antigen stimulation: H. pylori (gastric), Sjögren’s (salivary), Hashimoto’s (thyroid).
Gastric MALT lymphoma often regresses with H. pylori eradication.
Peyer’s patch M cells are the entry portal for Salmonella Typhi and prions.
